decks.title: Lifelines of National Economy — Part 1: Major Sea Ports and International Airports (board map work)
goals: Locate and label the ten major sea ports on the board map list
Locate and label the six international airports on the board map list
Identify each port from a clue about its harbour, cargo or position
Choose a suitable port for a given region or cargo

slides.heading: Lifelines of National Economy
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the part of this chapter that the board examines: the ten major sea ports and six international airports you must locate and label on the map of India.

visual.alt: Overview of Part 1: why ports and airports matter, five west-coast ports, five east-coast ports, six international airports, and clue-based practice
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance (board-assessed)

slides.narration: Namaste! In the board exam, this chapter is tested through map work only: ten major sea ports and six international airports. The rest of the chapter, on roads, railways, communication and trade, is for your interdisciplinary project, and Part 2 will help you with it. Here we will learn each port and airport with a clue that fixes it in your memory.

slides.heading: Gateways to the world
bullets: Most of India's foreign trade by volume moves by **sea**, through its **major ports**.
Each port serves a **hinterland**: the inland area whose goods it ships.
**International airports** carry passengers and light, valuable or urgent cargo.
The board list has **10 ports** (5 on each coast) and **6 airports**.

nodes.label: Farm, mine or factory in the hinterland
Road, rail or pipeline to the coast

visual.alt: Flow from a farm, mine or factory in the hinterland, by road, rail or pipeline to a major sea port, then by ship to world markets

slides.narration: Ports and airports are India's gateways to the world. A port is only as useful as the inland area it serves, its hinterland. Iron ore from Odisha leaves through Paradip; cotton yarn from Gujarat through Kandla. Airports carry people and light, valuable or urgent goods. As we go through the list, always ask: what is this port's clue, and what region does it serve?

slides.heading: Five major ports of the west coast (north to south)

rows: Tidal port at the head of the Gulf of Kachchh; built after Partition to replace Karachi
Biggest port; large, naturally sheltered harbour
On the Zuari estuary; main iron-ore exporting port of Goa
Exports iron-ore concentrate from the Kudremukh area
Extreme south-west; where a lagoon opens to the sea, giving a natural harbour

visual.alt: Table of five west-coast ports from north to south with state and clue: Kandla in Gujarat, Mumbai in Maharashtra, Marmagao in Goa, New Mangalore in Karnataka, and Kochi in Kerala

slides.narration: Start at the top of the west coast. Kandla, now called Deendayal Port, sits at the head of the Gulf of Kachchh and was built after Partition to replace Karachi. Mumbai is the biggest port, with a fine natural harbour. Marmagao in Goa and New Mangalore in Karnataka ship iron ore. Kochi, in the far south-west, sits at the mouth of a lagoon.

slides.heading: Quick check: the lagoon port
slides.narration: Think of the far south-west and its backwaters.

slides.heading: Five major ports of the east coast (south to north)

rows: Extreme south-east; natural harbour; trade with Sri Lanka and the Maldives
An early artificial harbour on the straight Coromandel coast
Deepest harbour almost enclosed by land, sheltered by hills; first built for iron-ore exports
Near the Mahanadi delta; known for shipping iron ore
Subsidiary port on the Hugli estuary, relieving the river port of Kolkata

visual.alt: Table of five east-coast ports from south to north with state and clue: Tuticorin and Chennai in Tamil Nadu, Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh, Paradip in Odisha, and Haldia in West Bengal

slides.narration: Now travel up the east coast. Tuticorin, in the extreme south-east, trades with Sri Lanka and the Maldives. Chennai has one of the oldest artificial harbours, because the Coromandel coast has few natural ones. Visakhapatnam is the deepest landlocked port, sheltered by hills. Paradip ships Odisha's iron ore. Haldia, on the Hugli estuary, eases the load on Kolkata, whose river port is hard for big ships to reach.

slides.heading: Quick check: the deepest landlocked port
slides.narration: Which east-coast port is tucked between hills?

slides.heading: Natural, artificial and river ports
columns:
**Natural harbours**

- Sheltered by the shape of the coast.
- **Mumbai**: large and naturally sheltered.
- **Kochi**: at a lagoon entrance.
- **Visakhapatnam**: landlocked among hills.

**Built or river-based**

- **Chennai**: one of the oldest **artificial** harbours, built on a straight coast.
- **Kandla**: a **tidal** port.
- **Haldia**: a **subsidiary** port downstream of Kolkata on the Hugli.

visual.alt: Table of harbour types with examples: natural, Mumbai and Kochi; landlocked, Visakhapatnam; artificial, Chennai; tidal, Kandla; subsidiary estuary port, Haldia

slides.narration: Ports differ in how nature helped them. Mumbai and Kochi have natural shelter, and Visakhapatnam hides among hills. Chennai's coast is straight and exposed, so its harbour had to be built. Kandla is a tidal port. Haldia was built near the mouth of the Hugli because silt makes it hard for large ships to reach Kolkata upstream. These features make excellent map clues.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: locating the west-coast ports
slides.body_md: Task: *On an outline map of India, locate and label the five major west-coast ports.*
bullets: Step 1 — Recall the order north to south: Kandla, Mumbai, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi.
Step 2 — Use state boundaries: Gujarat (Gulf of Kachchh), Maharashtra (Konkan coast), Goa (small coastal state), Karnataka (coast north of Mangaluru), Kerala (central coast).
Step 3 — Put each dot **on the coastline**, not inland or in the sea.
Step 4 — Write the name beside the dot, pointing the label out to sea so it stays readable.

rows: Eastern end of the Gulf of Kachchh
Placing it in the Gulf of Khambhat
Putting it at the southern tip

visual.alt: Table of west-coast port positions and common slips: Kandla at the eastern end of the Gulf of Kachchh, not the Gulf of Khambhat; Mumbai on the Konkan coast; Marmagao in Goa; New Mangalore in Karnataka, not Kerala; Kochi on the central Kerala coast, not the tip

slides.narration: Map marks are lost through small slips, so be careful. Learn the five ports in order from north to south. Use the states as anchors: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala. Put each dot exactly on the coastline. Do not put Kandla in the Gulf of Khambhat or New Mangalore in Kerala. Write each name clearly, with the label pointing out to sea.

slides.heading: Quick check: west-coast order
slides.body_md: Arrange the ports from north to south.
slides.narration: Begin in Gujarat and finish in Kerala.

slides.heading: Six international airports on the map list

rows: Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International (earlier Raja Sansi)
Northern Punjab, near the Pakistan border

visual.alt: Table of the six international airports with city, airport name and location: Amritsar, Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai at Meenambakkam, Kolkata and Hyderabad

slides.narration: Six international airports are on the board list. In the north-west, Amritsar near the Pakistan border and Delhi, the capital. On the coasts, Mumbai and Chennai, which are also major ports, and Kolkata on the Hugli. In the heart of the Deccan, Hyderabad. Learn each with its full name, because questions sometimes give the airport's name and ask for the city.

slides.heading: Quick check: Meenambakkam
slides.narration: Which coastal capital in the south has an airport at Meenambakkam?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: identifying ports from a source
slides.body_md: Source (written by SOYL): *"We left the port at the mouth of the Mahanadi with ore, sailed south past the landlocked harbour in the hills, and next morning entered the old artificial harbour of a southern capital."*
bullets: Step 1 — Mouth of the Mahanadi + ore → **Paradip**, Odisha.
Step 2 — Landlocked harbour in the hills → **Visakhapatnam**, Andhra Pradesh.
Step 3 — Old artificial harbour of a southern capital → **Chennai**, Tamil Nadu.
Step 4 — Direction: from Odisha to Tamil Nadu is **south** along the east coast.

visual.alt: Table matching source clues to ports: mouth of the Mahanadi with ore is Paradip in Odisha; landlocked harbour in the hills is Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh; old artificial harbour of a southern capital is Chennai in Tamil Nadu

slides.narration: Source questions on this chapter test whether you can recognise a port from its description. Underline each clue: the Mahanadi and ore mean Paradip; a landlocked harbour among hills means Visakhapatnam; an old artificial harbour in a southern capital means Chennai. Then check the direction. Moving from Odisha to Tamil Nadu, the ship is sailing south.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which port for which cargo?
slides.body_md: Task: *Suggest the nearest major port for (i) iron ore from Goa, (ii) cotton yarn from Ahmedabad, (iii) granite from southern Tamil Nadu.*
bullets: Step 1 — Find the state of each starting point.
Step 2 — Recall that state's major port on the list.
Step 3 — (i) **Marmagao**; (ii) **Kandla**; (iii) **Tuticorin**.
Step 4 — Give a reason: the nearest port on the same coast keeps land transport short and cheap.

visual.alt: Table of cargo, state and nearest major port: iron ore from Goa through Marmagao; cotton yarn from Ahmedabad through Kandla; granite from southern Tamil Nadu through Tuticorin

slides.narration: Here the map becomes a tool for reasoning. First find which state the cargo starts in. Then recall that state's major port. Goa's ore goes through Marmagao, Gujarat's yarn through Kandla, and southern Tamil Nadu's granite through Tuticorin. Always add the reason: a nearby port on the same coast keeps the costly land journey short.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Kandla, Mumbai, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi
Tidal (Kandla), biggest natural (Mumbai), lagoon (Kochi), artificial (Chennai), landlocked (Visakhapatnam), subsidiary (Haldia)
Amritsar, Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai (Meenambakkam), Kolkata, Hyderabad

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: west-coast and east-coast ports in order, their clues, and the six airports

slides.narration: To sum up. Five ports on each coast, learnt in order: Kandla, Mumbai, Marmagao, New Mangalore and Kochi on the west; Tuticorin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip and Haldia on the east. Each has a clue. And six international airports: Amritsar, Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata and Hyderabad. Practise them on a blank map until you can place all sixteen without looking.

slides.heading: Exam tips: map work
bullets: Practise on a **blank outline map** at least three times before the exam.
Ports go **on the coastline**; airports at the **city**.
Use a **neat dot** and the **full name**; one mark per place.
Common slips: **New Mangalore is in Karnataka**, **Tuticorin in Tamil Nadu**, **Haldia not Kolkata** for the port.
Kandla is now officially **Deendayal Port**; either name is accepted.
slides.narration: Some final tips. Map marks are among the easiest in the paper, but only if you practise on a blank map. Put ports exactly on the coastline and airports at their cities. Use a neat dot and the full name. Watch for the common slips: New Mangalore is in Karnataka, Tuticorin is in Tamil Nadu, and the port on the list is Haldia, not Kolkata.

decks.title: Lifelines of National Economy — Part 2: Transport, Communication and Trade (project companion, not board-assessed)
goals: Compare roadways, railways, pipelines, waterways and airways
Describe communication networks and their role
Explain international trade, balance of trade and tourism
Plan an interdisciplinary project on transport and the economy

slides.heading: Transport, Communication and Trade
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a companion for your **interdisciplinary project**. CBSE does not examine these topics in the board paper; they are assessed through the project.

visual.alt: Overview of Part 2: roadways, railways, pipelines, waterways, airways, communication, and trade and tourism
visual.caption: Project companion: not assessed in the board exam

slides.narration: This part is your project companion. The board exam does not test it, but your interdisciplinary project does, and it explains how the whole economy moves. Goods, people and ideas travel by road, rail, pipeline, water and air, and messages travel by post, phone and screen. Together these are the lifelines of the national economy.

slides.heading: Five modes of transport compared

rows: Short distances, door-to-door service, hilly terrain
Bulky goods and passengers over long distances
Hard to build in mountains and deserts
Crude oil, products and natural gas
Fast travel; remote and difficult terrain

visual.alt: Table comparing five modes of transport: roadways for short door-to-door trips; railways for bulky long-distance cargo; pipelines for oil and gas; waterways for cheap heavy cargo; airways for speed and remote areas, each with a limitation

slides.narration: Each mode of transport has its strengths. Roads give door-to-door service over short distances. Railways carry bulky goods and crowds of passengers over long distances. Pipelines move oil and gas cheaply once built. Waterways are the cheapest for heavy cargo. And air is the fastest, reaching places other modes cannot. A good transport system uses all of them together.

slides.heading: Roadways
bullets: **Golden Quadrilateral**: six-lane super highways linking **Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai**.
**North–South corridor**: Srinagar to Kanyakumari. **East–West corridor**: Silchar (Assam) to Porbandar (Gujarat).
Road types: **national highways**, **state highways**, **district roads**, **other (rural) roads**, **border roads** (Border Roads Organisation, set up in 1960), **international highways**.

visual.alt: Table of road types and who builds them: national highways by central agencies, state highways by state public works departments, district roads by Zila Parishads, rural roads by special schemes, and border roads by the Border Roads Organisation

slides.narration: Roads reach almost everywhere. The Golden Quadrilateral links India's four biggest metros with fast highways, and two long corridors cross the country north to south and east to west. Different bodies look after different roads, from national highways to village roads. The Border Roads Organisation builds roads in tough border areas, which matter for defence and remote communities.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Golden Quadrilateral
slides.narration: Which four big cities form the corners?

slides.heading: Railways and pipelines
bullets: **Railways** carry bulky goods and passengers over long distances; gauges are **broad (1.676 m)**, **metre (1 m)** and **narrow (0.762 m and 0.610 m)**.
The flat, fertile **northern plains** favour dense rail networks; the **Himalayas**, deserts and swampy areas make building hard.
**Pipelines** carry crude oil, petroleum products and gas from fields to refineries and plants, for example the **Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur** gas pipeline.
Pipelines cost much to lay, but running costs are low and **transshipment losses and delays** are avoided.

visual.alt: Table of railway gauges: broad gauge 1.676 metres, metre gauge 1 metre, narrow gauge 0.762 and 0.610 metres

slides.narration: Railways are India's workhorse for heavy goods and long journeys. Lines spread easily across the flat northern plains but struggle in mountains and deserts. Track comes in broad, metre and narrow gauges. Pipelines are a hidden network: once laid, they move oil and gas cheaply and continuously, without the losses of loading and unloading.

slides.heading: Quick check: pipelines
slides.narration: Think about what happens after the pipeline is laid.

slides.heading: Waterways and airways

rows: Kerala: West Coast Canal, Kottapuram to Kollam
Fastest; vital in the north-east; Pawan Hans helicopters serve offshore oil and remote areas

visual.alt: Table of waterways and airways: National Waterway 1 on the Ganga from Prayagraj to Haldia; National Waterway 2 on the Brahmaputra from Sadiya to Dhubri; National Waterway 3 on the Kerala West Coast Canal; and airways, fastest and vital in the north-east, with Pawan Hans helicopters

slides.narration: Water is the cheapest way to move heavy cargo, and it is kind to the environment. India's first three national waterways run on the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and the canals of Kerala. Airways are the fastest and most comfortable, and in the north-east, where rivers, forests and floods block roads, they are especially important. Helicopters even serve offshore oil platforms.

slides.heading: Quick check: National Waterway 1
slides.narration: Which river and which two end points?

slides.heading: Communication
bullets: **Postal network**: first-class mail (cards, envelopes) is **airlifted**; second-class mail (book packets, registered newspapers, periodicals) goes by **surface** transport.
Special **mail channels** speed up delivery in large towns and cities.
**Telecommunication** links cities and villages by phone and internet.
**Mass communication**: radio, television, newspapers, magazines and films inform and entertain; films are certified before release.

rows: Informs, educates and entertains large audiences
Fast exchange of information and services

visual.alt: Table of forms of communication and their roles: personal communication by post and phone, mass communication by radio, TV, print and film, and digital networks

slides.narration: Communication moves information the way transport moves goods. The postal system airlifts first-class mail and sends heavier mail by road and rail. Telephone and internet networks connect even remote villages. Radio, television, newspapers and films reach millions at once. For your project, think about how a farmer or a small shopkeeper uses these networks every day.

slides.heading: International trade and tourism

nodes.label: Tourism: earns foreign exchange, supports handicrafts, promotes national integration

visual.alt: Flow: exports and imports together give the balance of trade, which is favourable if exports exceed imports and unfavourable if imports exceed them; tourism separately earns foreign exchange and supports handicrafts

slides.narration: Trade is the exchange of goods between people and countries. When a country sells more abroad than it buys, its balance of trade is favourable; when it buys more, it is unfavourable. Tourism is trade too: visitors spend money here, which earns foreign exchange, supports handicraft workers and guides, and helps Indians from different regions understand each other.

slides.heading: Quick check: air transport in the north-east
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Why might roads and railways be hard to build there?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: calculating a balance of trade
slides.body_md: Data (imagined): *a country exports goods worth ₹720 thousand crore and imports goods worth ₹800 thousand crore.*
bullets: Step 1 — Balance of trade = exports − imports.
Step 2 — 720 − 800 = −80 thousand crore.
Step 3 — Imports exceed exports, so the balance is **unfavourable** by ₹80 thousand crore.
Step 4 — Interpret: the country must pay for the gap from other earnings, such as services or tourism.

visual.alt: Bar chart of imagined figures: exports of 720 and imports of 800 thousand crore rupees
visual.caption: Imagined figures. Bar 1: exports, 720. Bar 2: imports, 800.

slides.narration: Here is the one calculation this topic needs. Subtract imports from exports. Seven hundred and twenty minus eight hundred gives minus eighty. Because imports are larger, the balance is unfavourable by eighty thousand crore rupees. In your project, explain what such a gap means and how a country might pay for it, for example through services or tourism.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning your project
slides.body_md: Project idea (SOYL suggestion): *"How does one product reach my home?" Trace a packet of tea, a mobile phone or a bag of rice from where it is made to your local shop.*
bullets: Step 1 — Choose a product and find where it is produced.
Step 2 — Map the route: which modes of transport carry it, and through which port or airport if imported or exported.
Step 3 — Note the communication used: orders, payments, tracking.
Step 4 — Draw conclusions on cost, time and environmental impact, and suggest one improvement.

visual.alt: Flow of a project plan: product and origin, transport route and modes, ports or airports used, communication and payment, and conclusions with suggestions

slides.narration: A strong project tells a story. Pick a product you use and follow it from its source to your home. Which roads, railways, ships or planes carried it? Which port or airport did it pass through? How were orders and payments sent? End with your own conclusions about cost, time and pollution. That links geography, economics and your daily life, which is exactly what an interdisciplinary project wants.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Golden Quadrilateral; North–South and East–West corridors; road types
Long-distance, bulky goods; gauges; terrain limits
Oil and gas; low running cost; HVJ
Post, telecom, mass media; balance of trade; tourism

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: roadways, railways, pipelines, waterways, airways, and communication and trade

slides.narration: To sum up. Roads, railways, pipelines, waterways and airways each do a different job, and a modern economy needs them all. Communication moves information as fast as transport moves goods. Trade and tourism link India to the world. Remember, this part is for your project, while the board exam tests the ports and airports from Part 1.

slides.heading: Project tips
bullets: Keep a **clear question** and stick to it.
Use **maps, tables and photos you take yourself**; label sources honestly.
Use **dated** figures from official sources and say which year they are for.
Link at least **two subjects** (for example geography and economics).
Finish with **your own conclusions** and a practical suggestion.
slides.narration: A few tips for the project. Ask one clear question and keep to it. Draw your own maps and tables, and say where every fact comes from. Transport and trade figures change every year, so always give the year of any number you use. Link at least two subjects, and end with your own conclusion and a practical suggestion.

notes.title: Lifelines of National Economy — Notes

sections.heading: 1. What the board examines
sections.body_md:
In the CBSE board exam this chapter is examined **only through map work**: locating and labelling the **ten major sea ports** and **six international airports** below. The rest of the chapter (roadways, railways, pipelines, waterways, airways, communication, trade and tourism) is assessed through the **interdisciplinary project**; sections 4 and 5 of these notes support that project.

Most of India's foreign trade by volume moves through its **sea ports**; each port serves a **hinterland**, the inland area whose goods pass through it. International airports carry passengers and light, valuable or urgent cargo.

key_terms.definition_md: The inland area whose goods are shipped through a particular port.
A large port administered as a major port, handling most of the country's sea trade.

rows: Major sea ports and international airports (map work)

visual.alt: Table: map work on major ports and international airports is assessed in the board exam; transport, communication and trade are assessed through the interdisciplinary project

sections.heading: 2. Major sea ports (board map list)
sections.body_md:
**West coast, north to south**
- **Kandla (Deendayal Port), Gujarat:** a **tidal port** at the head of the **Gulf of Kachchh**, developed after independence to replace **Karachi** (which went to Pakistan) and serve north-western India.
- **Mumbai, Maharashtra:** the **biggest** port, with a large, **naturally sheltered** harbour.
- **Marmagao, Goa:** on the **Zuari** estuary; the main **iron-ore** exporting port of Goa.
- **New Mangalore, Karnataka:** exports **iron-ore concentrate** from the Kudremukh area.
- **Kochi, Kerala:** in the extreme south-west, at the entrance of a **lagoon**, with a natural harbour.

**East coast, south to north**
- **Tuticorin (V. O. Chidambaranar Port), Tamil Nadu:** in the extreme **south-east**; natural harbour; trade with **Sri Lanka and the Maldives**.
- **Chennai, Tamil Nadu:** one of the **oldest artificial** ports, on the straight Coromandel coast.
- **Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh:** the **deepest** harbour almost enclosed by land (**landlocked**), sheltered by hills, first built for **iron-ore** exports.
- **Paradip, Odisha:** near the **Mahanadi** delta; known for shipping **iron ore**.
- **Haldia, West Bengal:** a **subsidiary port** on the Hugli estuary, developed to relieve **Kolkata**, an inland river port that silt makes hard for large ships to reach.

key_terms.definition_md: A port where ship movements depend on the rise and fall of the tide, such as Kandla.
A harbour created by building breakwaters on an open coast, such as Chennai.
A harbour almost enclosed by land, giving very sheltered water, such as Visakhapatnam.

rows: Tidal; head of Gulf of Kachchh

visual.alt: Table of the ten major ports with state and clue

sections.heading: 3. International airports (board map list)
sections.body_md:
- **Amritsar** (Punjab): **Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee** International Airport, earlier known as **Raja Sansi**; near the Pakistan border.
- **Delhi**: **Indira Gandhi** International Airport.
- **Mumbai** (Maharashtra): **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj** International Airport.
- **Chennai** (Tamil Nadu): Chennai International Airport at **Meenambakkam**.
- **Kolkata** (West Bengal): **Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose** International Airport.
- **Hyderabad** (Telangana): **Rajiv Gandhi** International Airport.

Mumbai and Chennai are both **major sea ports** and international airports; Kolkata's port on the list is **Haldia**.

key_terms.definition_md: An airport with customs and immigration facilities for flights to and from other countries.

rows: Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee (Raja Sansi)

visual.alt: Table of the six international airports with their cities

sections.heading: 4. Transport (project topic)
sections.body_md:
*Not assessed in the board exam; for the interdisciplinary project.*
- **Roadways:** door-to-door service, cheaper to build than railways, suit hilly terrain and short distances. **Golden Quadrilateral** super highways link **Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai**; the **North–South corridor** joins **Srinagar and Kanyakumari**, the **East–West corridor** joins **Silchar (Assam) and Porbandar (Gujarat)**. Types: national highways, state highways (state PWDs), district roads (Zila Parishads), other rural roads, **border roads** (Border Roads Organisation, 1960), international highways.
- **Railways:** the main carrier of bulky goods and long-distance passengers; gauges **broad 1.676 m**, **metre 1 m**, **narrow 0.762 m and 0.610 m**; dense in the **northern plains**; difficult in the Himalayas, deserts and swampy areas.
- **Pipelines:** crude oil, petroleum products and gas from fields to refineries, fertiliser and power plants (e.g. the **Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur** gas pipeline); high initial cost, low running cost, no transshipment losses or delays.
- **Waterways:** cheapest, fuel-efficient and environment-friendly for heavy cargo. **NW 1**: Ganga, Prayagraj (Allahabad)–Haldia; **NW 2**: Brahmaputra, Sadiya–Dhubri; **NW 3**: West Coast Canal in Kerala, Kottapuram–Kollam (with Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals).
- **Airways:** fastest, most comfortable; reach mountains, deserts, forests and the **north-east**; **Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd.** serves ONGC offshore operations and remote areas.

key_terms.definition_md: Six-lane super highways joining Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai.
Moving cargo from one vehicle or mode to another during a journey.
A river or canal stretch developed for navigation and declared of national importance.

visual.alt: Table of five transport modes with an advantage and a limitation each

sections.heading: 5. Communication, trade and tourism (project topic)
sections.body_md:
*Not assessed in the board exam; for the interdisciplinary project.*
- **Postal network:** **first-class mail** (cards, envelopes) is airlifted between stations; **second-class mail** (book packets, registered newspapers, periodicals) goes by surface transport; special mail channels speed delivery in towns and cities.
- **Telecommunication** connects cities and villages; **mass communication** (radio, television, newspapers, magazines, films) informs, educates and entertains; films are certified before release.
- **Trade:** the exchange of goods between people, states and countries. **Balance of trade** = exports − imports; **favourable** when exports exceed imports, **unfavourable** when imports exceed exports.
- **Tourism:** promotes national integration, supports **handicrafts** and cultural pursuits, and earns **foreign exchange**.

key_terms.definition_md: The difference between the value of a country's exports and imports.
When the value of exports is greater than the value of imports.

visual.alt: Flow: exports and imports give the balance of trade, which is favourable when exports are larger and unfavourable when imports are larger

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes (map work)**
- Placing **New Mangalore** in Kerala (it is in **Karnataka**) or **Tuticorin** in Kerala (it is in **Tamil Nadu**).
- Marking **Kolkata** instead of **Haldia** for the port on the list.
- Putting **Kandla** in the Gulf of Khambhat instead of the **Gulf of Kachchh**.
- Dots inland for ports or in the sea for airports.

**How marks are awarded**
- One mark per place: correct location, clear dot, correct name (either current or older name accepted, e.g. Kandla or Deendayal Port).
- Source questions on this chapter ask you to identify ports from clues; use the clue table in section 2.
- Transport, communication and trade are assessed through the **project**, not the board paper.

questions.stem_md: Which major port lies at the head of the Gulf of Kachchh?

questions.stem_md: Kandla was developed soon after independence. Which reason best explains why?

questions.stem_md: An imagined ship is loading iron-ore concentrate from the Kudremukh area of the Western Ghats. At which major port in Karnataka is it most likely docked?

questions.stem_md: Which major port, in the extreme south-west, sits where a lagoon opens to the sea, giving it a natural harbour?

questions.stem_md: Which major port in the extreme south-east of India, in Tamil Nadu, has a natural harbour and trades with Sri Lanka and the Maldives?

questions.stem_md: Which major port on the Coromandel coast is among the earliest artificial harbours built in India?

questions.stem_md: Which port in Andhra Pradesh has the deepest harbour almost enclosed by land, sheltered by hills?

questions.stem_md: Haldia was developed as a subsidiary port. Which older port does it relieve, and why does that port need relief?

questions.stem_md: Using the map list of major ports, suggest one stretch of India's coast where a new major port could be useful. Justify your choice in five points.

answer.model_answer_md:

2. **Gap:** this is the longest east-coast stretch without a major port on the list, so cargo now travels far by land.
3. **Hinterland:** the fertile delta, Telangana and the **Deccan** produce rice, tobacco, cotton and manufactured goods that need an outlet.
4. **Links:** the region already has railways and highways that could feed a port, and **Hyderabad**'s international airport is within reach.
5. **Caution:** a delta coast has **silt** and cyclone risk, so the site needs deep water and protection, like Visakhapatnam's sheltered harbour.
